opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the applications I'm most excited about, partly because it's such a concrete clinical pain point. When you sequence a patient, you very often find variants where nobody can say whether they're pathogenic or benign. They sit in this gray zone, and that's frustrating for clinicians and really hard for families.

What's interesting about a model like Evo is that it was never explicitly trained to classify variants. It learned from enormous amounts of genomic sequence across the tree of life. But because it learned what "natural" or evolutionarily plausible sequence looks like, you can ask it how surprising a particular mutation is. If a variant makes the sequence look much less likely to the model, that's a signal it may be disrupting something functionally important. So you get a zero-shot predictor of variant effect, without curated labels for that gene or that disease.

We've seen encouraging results on known variants in genes like BRCA1, where the model can separate benign from likely pathogenic variants quite well, including noncoding and splice-region variants that protein-only models can't see. That's a big deal, because a lot of the genome's regulatory logic lives outside coding sequence, and that's where many variants of unknown significance sit.

I'd be careful not to oversell it. These scores aren't a diagnosis. They're a prior, a way to prioritize which variants deserve experimental follow-up or closer clinical attention. The real power comes from pairing the model with the lab: you make predictions, test them with high-throughput functional assays, and feed that data back in. Over time I think that loop can shrink the VUS problem dramatically. But it should augment clinical genetics, not replace the careful evidence-gathering that goes into a classification.

The bigger picture is that we're starting to have models that read DNA in a way that captures biological function, not just pattern matching on text. Variant interpretation is one of the first places where that pays off directly for patients.

r001.rationale: The response describes encouraging variant-prediction results and strengths on noncoding and splice-region variants, but does not characterize the model as roughly state of the art.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is honestly one of the things I'm most excited about, because variants of unknown significance are this enormous unsolved problem in clinical genetics. If you get your genome sequenced today, you'll come back with hundreds of variants where the honest answer from a clinician is "we don't know." ClinVar is full of these. And the reason is that for most of the genome, we've never had a way to actually read the sequence and say what a change does. We've relied on population frequency, conservation, maybe a lab assay if someone happened to study that gene.

What a genomic language model like Evo lets you do is approach it from a totally different angle. The model has been trained on, you know, trillions of nucleotides across the tree of life, and in doing that it has to learn the grammar of DNA. It learns what a functional promoter looks like, what a splice site looks like, what a protein coding sequence that actually folds looks like. So when you give it a variant, you can just ask it: how likely is this sequence relative to the reference? And it turns out that likelihood shift is a surprisingly good signal for whether the variant is going to break something, and importantly it works zero-shot, without us ever training on labeled clinical data.

The part I find really compelling is that it's not just coding variants. Most of the tools that exist today, like protein language models, are great for missense mutations in proteins, but the majority of the genome is noncoding, and that's where the VUS problem is actually worst. A DNA-level model can score a variant in a regulatory region or in an intron in the same framework, because it's operating on the raw nucleotide sequence rather than on an annotated protein.

Now, I want to be careful here. The model is giving you a prior, not a diagnosis. The way I think about it is that it compresses what evolution has already told us, and evolution is a very long-running experiment on which sequences are tolerated. But a variant being disfavored by evolution isn't the same as it causing a specific disease in a specific person. So in practice I see this as a triage tool: you take ten thousand VUS, the model tells you which few hundred are most likely to matter, and then you go validate those experimentally, ideally with pooled screens where you can test lots of them at once. That loop, model proposes and the lab tests, is where I think it gets really powerful, because every round of validation also gives you data to make the model better.

r001.rationale: The response describes Evo as a promising way to score variants and contrasts DNA-level models with existing protein language models, but it never characterizes the model as roughly state of the art.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s one of the most exciting potential applications. When you sequence someone’s genome, you find variants where we simply don’t know what they do. The question is whether a model can help us distinguish a change that’s relatively benign from one that disrupts an important biological function.

One way to approach that is to compare how the model evaluates the original sequence and the sequence containing the variant. That can give you a signal about whether the change is consequential, including in noncoding regions, where interpretation is particularly challenging.

But predicting that a variant affects biology isn’t the same as establishing that it causes a patient’s disease. You still need experimental validation and clinical context. So I see these models as a way to prioritize variants and generate testable hypotheses, with the potential to make that interpretation process much more effective.

r001.rationale: The response describes models as potentially useful for prioritizing variants and assessing consequences, but it does not characterize their performance as roughly state of the art.

sol-6.1.text:
I think this is one of the most exciting potential applications. When you sequence someone’s genome, you find variants where we simply don’t know whether they matter. A model could help prioritize those variants by asking how a particular change affects its predictions about the surrounding sequence.

But there’s an important distinction between predicting that a variant affects biological function and showing that it causes disease. A variant might have an effect in one cell type or one context and not another. So I’d view these models as tools for generating hypotheses and directing experiments. Ultimately, you want to connect those predictions to experimental measurements and clinical evidence before using them to guide someone’s care.

r001.rationale: The response describes models as potentially useful for prioritizing variants and generating hypotheses, but does not characterize their ability as roughly state of the art.
